Tell me about the most complex GCP envir: Pick the environment with the most genuine complexity (multiple teams/projects, multi-region, regulatory constraints, or a difficult migration) and structure the answer around scale (project/service count), the hardest architectural decision you made, and your specific ownership versus the team's - concrete numbers and named services make this far more credible than a general description.
What was the overall architecture of tha: Walk it top-down: how traffic enters (load balancers, Cloud CDN), the compute layer (GKE/Cloud Run/Compute Engine and why that mix), the data layer (Cloud SQL/BigQuery/Spanner), and the networking/security boundary (VPC design, IAM structure) - a clear layered description signals you actually understand the whole system, not just the piece you touched most.
What GCP native services did you design: Name the specific services and the reason each was chosen over alternatives (e.g. Cloud Spanner for global strong consistency versus Cloud SQL for a simpler regional relational need, Pub/Sub for decoupling asynchronous workflows) - justifying the choice demonstrates architectural reasoning, not just service familiarity.
How did you handle multi-tenancy or isol: Describe the actual isolation boundary used - separate GCP projects per team (strongest isolation, own IAM/quota/billing), separate namespaces within a shared GKE cluster with ResourceQuotas and NetworkPolicies (lighter-weight, shared infra cost), or a mix based on workload sensitivity - and the tradeoff reasoning behind the choice (blast radius vs. operational overhead).
Walk me through how you administered a p: Structure chronologically: initial cluster design decisions (regional vs. zonal, node pool strategy, network mode), the provisioning method (Terraform), then day-two concerns - upgrades, scaling, monitoring setup, incident response, and cost optimization - showing the full operational lifecycle, not just the initial build.
How did you handle node pool upgrades wi: Use surge upgrades (provisioning extra nodes before draining old ones) combined with PodDisruptionBudgets ensuring enough replicas stay available during voluntary node drains, and a multi-zone/regional cluster so upgrades roll through zones sequentially rather than all at once - test the upgrade path in staging first to catch API deprecations before they hit production.
What autoscaling strategy did you implem: Combine HPA (scaling Pod replicas based on CPU/custom metrics matched to the workload's actual bottleneck) with Cluster Autoscaler (scaling node count based on unschedulable Pods) - explain the specific metric choice for HPA (why CPU vs. request-based) and any node pool segmentation (separate pools for batch vs. latency-sensitive workloads) as the reasoning behind the overall strategy.
Can you describe a time when a human err: Use STAR, and be genuinely honest about the error (a bad config applied, a resource limit set wrong) rather than deflecting blame - the interviewer is testing accountability and learning from mistakes as much as the technical resolution itself.
How did you identify the root cause of t: Narrate the actual diagnostic sequence in order - what you checked first (dashboards/alerts), what that pointed to next (logs, recent changes), and how you confirmed the actual cause versus just the first plausible theory - concrete specificity here is what makes the story credible.
How did you resolve the issue?: Describe the specific fix (a rollback, a config correction, a resource limit adjustment) and how you verified it was actually resolved (metrics returning to baseline, not just the immediate symptom stopping) rather than assuming the fix worked.
What preventive measures did you impleme: Name a concrete, systemic prevention - a new automated check/validation gate in CI/CD, an added alert, a runbook, or a policy-as-code guardrail - since 'we were more careful after that' isn't a real prevention measure; a good answer shows the fix was structural, not just increased vigilance.
How did you manage networking within a K: Describe the CNI plugin used (or GKE's native networking), how NetworkPolicies were used to restrict Pod-to-Pod traffic by namespace/label (default-deny plus explicit allow rules), and how Services/Ingress handled internal and external traffic routing - specificity on NetworkPolicy design signals real security-conscious networking experience.
How did you manage networking between mu: Options to describe: VPC-native clusters with routes/peering between them for direct Pod-to-Pod reachability, a multi-cluster service mesh (Istio multi-cluster) for cross-cluster service discovery and mTLS, or simpler API-gateway-based integration where clusters only communicate through defined external endpoints rather than direct network-level connectivity - the choice depends on how tightly coupled the clusters' workloads actually need to be.
How did you implement end-to-end observa: Describe the three pillars working together: metrics (Prometheus/Cloud Monitoring) for aggregate health and alerting, structured logging (Cloud Logging) correlated by request/trace ID, and distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) tying a request's full path across services together - emphasize that the value comes from correlating all three during an actual incident, not each existing in isolation.
What metrics did you monitor?: Group by RED (rate, errors, duration) for services and USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources, plus business-specific metrics relevant to the system (queue depth, job success rate) - naming the actual metric names/dashboards used shows real operational familiarity versus reciting the framework names alone.
What logging strategy did you implement?: Structured (JSON) logs with consistent fields (timestamp, severity, service name, trace ID) shipped to a centralized system, with log levels used deliberately (not everything at INFO) and retention/cost policies tuned per log type (debug logs short retention, audit logs long retention) - mention how logs were made searchable/correlated with traces via the shared trace ID field.
How did you implement distributed tracin: Instrument services with an OpenTelemetry SDK (auto-instrumentation where available, manual spans for custom logic), propagate trace context across service boundaries via standard headers, and export to a tracing backend (Jaeger/Tempo/Cloud Trace) - describe one concrete case where tracing let you pinpoint latency in a specific service that metrics alone couldn't localize.
How do you define an SLI?: A Service Level Indicator is a specific, quantitative measure of a service's behavior - e.g. the proportion of successful HTTP requests, or the 95th-percentile request latency - chosen because it directly reflects what users actually experience, not just an easy-to-measure infrastructure metric.
How do you define an SLO?: A Service Level Objective is a target value or range for an SLI over a defined window - e.g. '99.9% of requests succeed over a rolling 30 days' - set based on what users actually need and what's realistically achievable, and used internally to guide engineering priorities (an SLO breach or shrinking error budget should influence whether the team focuses on reliability work versus new features).
How do you define an SLA?: A Service Level Agreement is an external, often contractual commitment to a customer about service performance, usually with financial or business consequences for missing it - SLAs are typically set looser than internal SLOs (e.g. a 99.9% SLA backed by a 99.95% internal SLO) so there's buffer to catch and fix issues before the customer-facing commitment is actually breached.
Give a concrete example of an SLA/SLO th: Describe a specific service, the SLI chosen (e.g. request success rate), the SLO target set and why (based on historical baseline plus business requirement), and how the error budget derived from it was actually used operationally (e.g. freezing risky releases when the error budget for the month was mostly consumed) - the operational usage detail is what proves it was a real, acted-upon SLO rather than a number on a dashboard nobody looked at.
How did you build your CI/CD pipeline fo: Describe them as two related but distinct pipelines: an infrastructure pipeline (Terraform plan/apply gated by review, triggered on infra repo changes) and an application pipeline (build, test, containerize, deploy, triggered on app repo changes) - explain how they're sequenced when both are needed (infra changes typically applied before the application that depends on them deploys).
Walk me through the pipeline from develo: Commit triggers CI (build, unit test, security scan) on the PR; merge to main triggers a build of a versioned artifact/image; that image deploys automatically to staging for integration testing; promotion to production is gated (manual approval or automated canary analysis) with automated rollback if post-deploy health checks fail - naming the actual tools at each stage grounds this concretely.
What CI/CD tools did you use?: List with the specific role each played - build/test orchestration (Jenkins, GitHub Actions), artifact storage (Artifact Registry), and deployment (ArgoCD for GitOps, or direct Helm/kubectl from the pipeline) - depth on how they connect together matters more than the tool list itself.
How did you handle secrets and environme: Secrets never live in the pipeline definition or repo - sourced from the CI/CD platform's own secret store or a dedicated secrets manager (Secret Manager, Vault) and injected as environment variables scoped to the specific job/stage that needs them, masked from logs automatically. Non-sensitive environment-specific config (URLs, feature flags) is handled separately via environment-specific config files or ConfigMaps.
How did you version your application art: Tag images with the Git commit SHA (immutable, traceable back to exact source) rather than a mutable tag like `latest`, optionally combined with semantic version tags for releases - this ensures every deployed artifact is unambiguously traceable to the exact code that produced it, which matters for both rollback and incident investigation.
How did you implement rollback for appli: Roll back by redeploying the previous known-good image tag/commit SHA through the same pipeline used for forward deploys (`kubectl rollout undo`, `helm rollback`, or reverting the Git commit in a GitOps-managed repo) - never a manual ad hoc fix under pressure - which requires keeping previous versions readily available (images retained in the registry, prior Helm release history intact).
How did you implement rollback for infra: Since Terraform's 'rollback' is really just applying the previous configuration version, this means reverting the Git commit that introduced the problematic change and re-running `terraform plan`/`apply` from that reverted state - which is why keeping infrastructure changes small and incremental (rather than large batched changes) matters, since a small change is much easier to safely revert than a sprawling one.
Have you provisioned GPU or TPU node poo: Answer honestly with specifics - which accelerator type (NVIDIA T4/A100, or GCP TPUs), whether you configured the node pool yourself (accelerator type/count, taints to keep non-GPU workloads off expensive nodes) or just deployed workloads onto an existing GPU pool.
Have you worked with Vertex AI endpoints: Answer with actual scope - whether you deployed/managed Vertex AI Endpoints yourself (model upload, endpoint creation, traffic splitting for canary) or primarily consumed an endpoint someone else set up, and any monitoring/scaling configuration you touched.
How did you provision GPU-enabled GKE no: Create a node pool specifying the accelerator type and count per node (`--accelerator type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=1`), install the NVIDIA device plugin DaemonSet (or use GKE's automatic driver installation) so Kubernetes can schedule against GPU resources, and taint the GPU node pool so only GPU-requesting Pods (with a matching toleration) get scheduled there, keeping expensive GPU nodes from being consumed by unrelated workloads.
How did you manage GPU scheduling and re: Set explicit GPU resource requests/limits on Pods (`nvidia.com/gpu: 1`) so the scheduler places them only on nodes with available GPU capacity, use taints/tolerations to reserve GPU nodes exclusively for GPU workloads, and consider node auto-provisioning or a separate autoscaling node pool specifically for GPU workloads so GPU capacity scales independently from general compute.
How did you control GPU infrastructure c: Use preemptible/spot GPU instances for fault-tolerant training workloads (significant cost savings, with checkpointing to handle preemption), scale GPU node pools to zero when idle rather than keeping them warm, right-size the accelerator type to the actual workload (not defaulting to the largest GPU available), and monitor utilization closely since idle GPU capacity is expensive and easy to over-provision.
How did you deploy and manage models usi: Upload the trained model artifact to the Vertex AI Model Registry, deploy it to an Endpoint (specifying machine type and autoscaling min/max replicas), and use traffic splitting to canary a new model version against the current one before fully promoting - Vertex AI handles the underlying serving infrastructure, autoscaling, and monitoring integration.
What metrics did you monitor for AI/ML i: Infrastructure-level (endpoint latency, error rate, GPU utilization) alongside model-level (prediction distribution, confidence score distribution, and accuracy/F1 once ground truth becomes available) and data-level (feature drift via PSI/KL divergence) - monitoring only the infrastructure layer misses the failure mode where a model is fast and healthy but quietly wrong.
If a data scientist or ML engineer asks: What does the model actually expect as input (schema, format, preprocessing steps) and what does 'correct' output look like, since without that contract you can't build a serving layer, validate inputs, or set up meaningful monitoring - this handoff detail is usually the biggest source of production issues if skipped.
What additional information would you ga: The artifact format and expected runtime/library versions (to match training exactly), expected request volume/latency requirements, the evaluation metrics and acceptable performance thresholds, and how the data science team wants drift/performance monitored in production - gathering this upfront avoids rework after the model is already deployed with mismatched assumptions.
What infrastructure would you provision: A serving layer (Vertex AI Endpoint or a containerized FastAPI wrapper on GKE) with autoscaling sized to expected traffic, a feature pipeline feeding it fresh input data, a model registry entry for versioning, monitoring for both infra and model-quality metrics, and a CI/CD path for future model version promotion with canary/rollback support - the same production discipline as any other service, plus the model-specific monitoring layer.
Are you using any AI tools in your day-t: Answer honestly and specifically - naming actual tools used (an AI coding assistant, an LLM for drafting runbooks/documentation, a chatbot for quick lookups) rather than a vague 'yes, sometimes,' since this question is checking genuine current adoption, not just awareness that such tools exist.
How do you use AI tools in your daily wo: Describe concrete use cases - drafting boilerplate code or tests faster, summarizing a long log/incident timeline, explaining an unfamiliar piece of code or error message, or drafting documentation - and be honest about where you still verify/don't fully trust the output, since blind trust in AI output is itself a red flag interviewers listen for.
Can you give a practical example of how: Pick one specific, measurable instance - e.g. 'drafting a Terraform module skeleton that would have taken 30 minutes took 5, then I reviewed and adjusted it' - concrete before/after framing is far more convincing than a general productivity claim.
How do you ensure AI-generated code or r: Treat AI output the same as any other untrusted first draft - code review by a human, running it through the full test suite and security/dependency scanning, and never accepting infrastructure or security-relevant suggestions without independently verifying they're actually correct for your specific context, since AI models can produce plausible-looking but subtly wrong or outdated recommendations.
How do you think the Platform Engineer/D: The role shifts toward higher-leverage work - less manual toil (routine config, boilerplate scripting increasingly AI-assisted) and more focus on the things AI can't easily do: architectural judgment, security/compliance review, and building the guardrails and platforms that let AI-assisted work happen safely at scale. Expect growing overlap with MLOps/LLMOps skills as more systems incorporate AI components that need the same production rigor (monitoring, CI/CD, security) as traditional services.
What new responsibilities do you think P: Operating the infrastructure and guardrails for AI/agentic systems specifically - GPU/accelerator infrastructure, model serving and versioning, LLM-specific monitoring (drift, cost, hallucination rate), and security controls unique to AI systems (prompt injection defense, agent action approval gates) - essentially extending existing platform engineering discipline to a new class of workload with its own operational quirks.
Do you think AI will replace DevOps engi: AI is more likely to automate specific tasks (boilerplate scripting, routine troubleshooting suggestions) than replace the role outright, since production systems still need human judgment for architectural decisions, incident accountability, and understanding business context AI doesn't have - the realistic shift is DevOps engineers spending less time on repetitive toil and more time on the judgment-heavy, higher-leverage parts of the job, similar to how earlier automation waves (config management, IaC) changed but didn't eliminate the role.
